claims.text: Nutrition and inpatient clinics serve as recognized entry points for routine infant HIV testing, and HIV testing may be integrated with services such as nutrition counselling.

When an infant or child has an unknown HIV status or exposure, health workers should assess for HIV exposure (including testing the mother with an RDT if her status is untested/unknown) and test the child to establish their HIV status and guide appropriate treatment or care.

claims.text: HIV testing services should not be restricted solely to health facilities; entry points include both facility-based and community-based testing outside of facilities (such as outreach, community-based services, workplaces, clubs, and bars).

Community-based HIV testing services can be delivered across multiple settings, including places of worship, educational establishments, workplaces, and mobile testing units such as vans or temporary testing facilities.
HIV self-testing is recognized as an approach that can be offered in the community as well as at health facilities.
Testing approaches also encompass provider-assisted referrals (such as index testing or assisted partner notification) and social network-based testing approaches.

results.question: Is clinic-based HIV testing enough, or should testing also be offered outside health facilities?

claims.text: In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status should be offered HIV testing in outpatient and immunization clinics.
HIV testing for infants and children may be integrated with other routine health services, such as during immunization or nutrition counselling.

results.question: Should immunization and outpatient clinics be offering HIV tests to children who have never been tested?

claims.text: An infant or child's exposure to HIV is determined through the mother.
Exposure status is classified as unknown if it is not known whether the infant or child was exposed, such as when the mother's HIV status is unknown.
Determining maternal HIV status involves ordering and conducting an HIV test for the mother using a testing algorithm.
An infant or child is categorized as not exposed when not known to have been exposed to HIV.

claims.text: For infants and children younger than 18 months of age, nucleic acid testing (NAT) / virological testing is indicated to diagnose HIV infection.

In infants and children under 18 months of age, NAT should be performed at various time points (including birth testing where of value, at six weeks, and at nine months) and should be used to confirm infection.
Same-day point-of-care NAT should be considered and prioritized for infant diagnosis at all relevant time points.

claims.text: For cisgender women at substantial risk of HIV infection, non-daily pill PrEP options include the dapivirine vaginal ring (DVR) as an additional prevention choice in combination prevention approaches, as well as long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA).

If a client declines or is not suitable for daily medication, healthcare providers may counsel on risk and alternative prevention options, as well as promote and provide male and female condoms and condom-compatible lubricants.
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) can be offered if there has been a suspected exposure to HIV within the preceding 72 hours.
Harm reduction services, including needle and syringe programmes and opioid substitution therapy, should be offered if the individual injects drugs.
Additional supporting services for individuals at elevated risk include STI screening and treatment, behavioural risk-reduction interventions, and regular HIV retesting (at least annually).

claims.text: DTG (dolutegravir) is the preferred third drug for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
When DTG is not available, ATV/r, DRV/r, LPV/r, or RAL may be considered as alternative third drug options for PEP.
NVP must not be used for PEP in adults, adolescents, and older children due to the risk of life-threatening serious adverse events.
